--- title: "2.1 Interpretation with Marginal Effects" --- - A marginal effect is your model's answer to a counterfactual question: - *If the value of this independent variable were different, how would the predicted outcome change?* - Every marginal effect is an answer to some "what if" question you pose to your fitted model - A **marginal effect** is defined as: - *The predicted change in the outcome for a change in* $x_{k}$ *of δ, holding other predictors constant* - And is calculated as the difference between two model predictions ($\eta$) - With nonlinearities, it is often the best choice to provide a **summary of the effect** of a variable ### Marginal effects with linear additive effects - In the special case of a linear regression model with linear, non-interactive (i.e., additive) effects: ${ME}_{x_{k} + 1} = \beta_{x_{k}}$ - This is only true in this incredibly limited situation ![](images/linear-effects-betas.png){width=60% fig-alt="A straight regression line with normal error distributions at several values of x; each one-unit increase in x raises y by beta."} #### Marginal effects with nonlinear and/or interactive effects - Marginal effects are most useful for nonlinear and/or interactive effects - In these cases, the marginal effects are summarizing different information than the coefficients ## Marginal effects defined - Denote our focal IV as $x_{k}$ - Denote the control variables as $\mathbf{x}_{- k}$ (all other IVs in the model excluding $x_{k}$) - A marginal effect, at its simplest, is the difference between two predictions (denoted as $\eta$ "eta"): one at a starting value of substantive interest; one at an ending value of substantive interest - Formally: $$ME = \eta\left( x_{k} = end,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{*}} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = start,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{*}} \right)$$ - Starting and ending values of the focal IV $x_{k}$ can be any values of substantive interest. For binary IVs, there are only two logical choices: 0 and 1 $${ME}_{binary} = \eta\left( x_{k} = 1,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{*}} \right) - \eta\left( x_{k} = 0,\ \mathbf{x}_{- k} = \mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{*}} \right)$$ - For example, can compare a prediction for no degree (=0) to college (=1) ### Marginal effects for continuous IVs - For continuous IVs, there are many more choices for starting and ending values. Common choices: - *start* = mean of $x_{k}$ - *end* = mean + 1 - *end* = mean + SD is also common\*; sometimes more informative - Any other values of substantive interest can be used for *start* and *end* (e.g., age 30 and age 55) - This flexibility is one of the benefits of using marginal effects for interpretation #### Amount of change ($\delta$) - There are two types of marginal effects for continuous IVs, differing in the amount of change $\delta$ ([Mize and Han 2026](/research/mize_han_hdma_2025.qmd)) - *Discrete change* in $\widehat{y}$ as an IV changes by a fixed amount - E.g., A one unit increase; a standard deviation increase - *Instantaneous rate of change* in $\widehat{y}$ (first derivative; AKA *slopes*) - Rates of changes are less intuitive to interpret and thus less popular in most social science applications \*In most applications, especially for large changes, I recommend centering the change on *start* value ## Terminology is confusing *"Mathematics is the art of giving the same name to different things."* -- Henri Poincaré - I use **marginal effects** as an umbrella term for all of these effects (i.e., both discrete and rates of changes), regardless of the specific amount of change - "Marginal" comes from the idea of evaluating a change at the margin---that is, asking what happens to an outcome when a predictor changes slightly, holding other things constant - Instantaneous rates of changes (AKA slopes) are sometimes called partial effects or (even more confusing) *marginal* changes ![](images/first-derivative.png){width=75% fig-alt="Two curves with tangent lines: where the tangent line has a negative slope the function is decreasing; where it has a positive slope the function is increasing."} ## Example: Occupational Prestige Data is from pooled General Social Survey (GSS) data from 1972 -- 2016 ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss", clear (cda_gss.dta | GSS 1972-2021 CDA - Categorical Data Analysis | date created 202 > 3) . . hist occprest, percent fcol(none) ylab(0(2)10) (bin=47, start=12, width=1.5744681) ``` ![](fig/cda-02_01_a-me_linear-0.png){width=80% fig-alt="Histogram of occupational prestige scores."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(haven) # import Stata data and labels library(dplyr) # data manipulation library(ggplot2) # graphs library(modelsummary) # regression tables library(marginaleffects) # predictions and marginal effects library(cleanplots) # graph scheme cleanplots_defaults() gss <- read_dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/cda_gss.dta") # Keep only model vars and drop any missing data on them gss <- gss[c("occprest", "age", "woman", "college")] gss <- gss[complete.cases(gss), ] # Treat binary variables as factors using their value labels gss <- gss |> mutate(woman = as_factor(woman), college = as_factor(college)) ggplot(gss, aes(occprest)) + geom_histogram(fill = NA, color = "black") + labs(x = "Occupational prestige") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-1-marginal-effects_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-alt='Histogram of occupational prestige scores.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Example occupational prestige scores - A [2018 *ASR* article](http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/0003122418761857) examining occupational prestige scores - The list of scores for various occupations can be [found here](http://ibgwww.colorado.edu/~agross/NNSD/prestige%20scores.html). Some examples: | Occupation | Prestige score | |:--------------------------|------:| | Elementary school teachers | 64.08 | | Sociologists | 60.75 | | "Sociology teachers" | 73.51 | | Statisticians | 55.57 | | Architects | 73.15 | | Physicians | 86.05 | | Registered nurses | 66.48 | | Sales workers, shoes | 27.67 | | Bartenders | 24.53 | | Barbers | 35.71 | | Parking lot attendants | 21.22 | ### Regression results for occupational prestige (DV) ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . regress occprest c.age i.woman i.college Source | SS df MS Number of obs = 58,304 -------------+---------------------------------- F(3, 58300) = 6232.46 Model | 2765051.56 3 921683.852 Prob > F = 0.0000 Residual | 8621657.35 58,300 147.884346 R-squared = 0.2428 -------------+---------------------------------- Adj R-squared = 0.2428 Total | 11386708.9 58,303 195.302281 Root MSE = 12.161 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- occprest | Coefficient Std. err. t P>|t| [95% conf. interval] --------------+---------------------------------------------------------------- age | 0.041 0.003 14.027 0.000 0.035 0.047 | woman | Women | -0.178 0.101 -1.756 0.079 -0.376 0.021 | college | College De.. | 16.422 0.121 136.142 0.000 16.185 16.658 _cons | 36.621 0.157 233.710 0.000 36.314 36.928 ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- . . esttab, b(2) se(2) nobase label /// > title("[2.1.b] Occupational Prestige Based on Age, Gender, and Education") [2.1.b] Occupational Prestige Based on Age, Gender, and Education ------------------------------------ (1) Occupation~e ------------------------------------ age of respondent 0.04*** (0.00) Women -0.18 (0.10) College Degree 16.42*** (0.12) Constant 36.62*** (0.16) ------------------------------------ Observations 58304 ------------------------------------ Standard errors in parentheses * p<0.05, ** p<0.01, *** p<0.001 ``` ## To visualize regression coefficients, I recommend [**coefplot**](https://repec.sowi.unibe.ch/stata/coefplot/getting-started.html). In R, I recommend [modelsummary](https://modelsummary.com/) for both. ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . qui margins woman, at(age=(20(5)80)) . marginsplot, /// > recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(38(2)46) /// > title("[2.1.c] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", siz > e(medium)) /// > ytitle("Occupational Prestige") Variables that uniquely identify margins: age woman ``` ![](fig/cda-02_01_c-me_linear-1.png){width=80% fig-alt="Predicted occupational prestige by age for men and women: two nearly overlapping straight lines rising slowly with age."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions(linmod, by = c("age", "woman"), newdata = datagrid(age = seq(20, 80, 5), woman = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(38, 46, 2), limits = c(38, 46)) + labs(title = "[2.1.c] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", x = "Age", y = "Occupational Prestige") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-1-marginal-effects_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-alt='Predicted occupational prestige by age for men and women: two nearly overlapping straight lines rising slowly with age.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Calculating marginal effects $$\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*{age}_{i} - 0.183*{woman}_{i} + 16.43*{college}_{i}$$ **To calculate the marginal effect of age, where should we hold the other variables constant?** Calculate the effect of aging from 40 to 50 for women without college degrees: $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0$ = 38.047 $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*50 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0$ = 38.447 38.447 -- 38.047 = 0.400 Calculate the effect of aging from 40 to 50 for women with college degrees: $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1$ = 54.477 $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*50 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1$ = 54.877 54.877 -- 54.477 = 0.400 ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . di 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0 38.047 . di 36.63 + 0.04*50 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0 38.447 . di 38.447 - 38.047 .4 . . di 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1 54.477 . di 36.63 + 0.04*50 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1 54.877 . di 54.877 - 54.477 .4 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 38.047 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*50 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 38.447 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 38.447 - 38.047 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 0.4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 54.477 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*50 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 54.877 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 54.877 - 54.477 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 0.4 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Simple interpretation due to linearity #### Continuous variables - Interpretation: **for a unit increase in *x~k~* the expected change in *y* is ME, holding other variables constant** - Remember, in the case of linear additive effects in linear regression: ${ME}_{x_{k} + 1} = \beta_{x_{k}}$ > *For each additional year a person ages, their job prestige is expected to be 0.04 points higher, holding other variables constant* > > *For ten additional years of age, a person's job prestige is expected to increase by 0.4 points, holding other variables constant* **Note:** 0.04 \* 10 = 0.40 Plot the effects for women, separately for those who went to college or not: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . qui margins, at(age=(20(5)90) woman=(1) college=(0 1)) . marginsplot, /// > recastci(rline) ciopts(lpat(dash) col(gs12)) ylab(35(5)60) /// > title("[2.1.d] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", siz > e(medium)) /// > subtitle("Women Respondents Only", size(medium)) /// > ytitle("Occupational Prestige") Variables that uniquely identify margins: age college ``` ![](fig/cda-02_01_d-me_linear-3.png){width=80% fig-alt="Predicted occupational prestige by age for women with and without a college degree: two parallel straight lines about 16 points apart."} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions(linmod, by = c("age", "college"), newdata = datagrid(age = seq(20, 90, 5), woman = "Women", college = unique, grid_type = "counterfactual")) + scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(35, 60, 5), limits = c(35, 60)) + labs(title = "[2.1.d] Predicted Occupational Prestige Based on Person's Age", subtitle = "Women Respondents Only", x = "Age", y = "Occupational Prestige") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](2-1-marginal-effects_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-alt='Predicted occupational prestige by age for women with and without a college degree: two parallel straight lines about 16 points apart.' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: ### Calculating marginal effects for a binary variable $$\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*{age}_{i} - 0.183*{woman}_{i} + 16.43*{college}_{i}$$ Calculate the effect of having a college degree for a 40-year-old woman: $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0$ = 38.047 $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1$ = 54.477 54.477 -- 38.047 = 16.43 Calculate the effect of having a college degree for a 40-year-old man: $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*0 + 16.43*0$ = 38.23 $\widehat{occprest} = 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*0 + 16.43*1$ = 54.66 54.66 -- 38.23 = 16.43 ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## Stata ```{.stata-run} . di 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0 38.047 . di 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1 54.477 . di 54.477 - 38.047 16.43 . . di 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*0 + 16.43*0 38.23 . di 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*0 + 16.43*1 54.66 . di 54.66 - 38.23 16.43 ``` ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 38.047 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*1 + 16.43*1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 54.477 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 54.477 - 38.047 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 16.43 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*0 + 16.43*0 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 38.23 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 36.63 + 0.04*40 - 0.183*0 + 16.43*1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 54.66 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} 54.66 - 38.23 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` r-output [1] 16.43 ``` ::: ::: ::: ### Interpreting binary variables coded as 0 and 1 - Interpretation: **having characteristic *x~k~* (as opposed to not having the characteristic) results in an expected change of ME in *y*, holding other variables constant** - Note these are usually group comparisons. Interpretations are more natural when you state these as comparisons - Again, in the case of linear additive effects: ${ME}_{x_{k} + 1} = \beta_{x_{k}}$ > *On average, those with college degrees hold jobs that are 16.43 points more prestigious than jobs held by those without a college degree (accounting for other factors)*
